translation_loss.what_was_lost: The translation renders 'duniya ki sawari' as 'traveler of the world', which loses the literal sense of 'sawari' as a passenger, ride, or procession, which directly links to the palanquin (doli) imagery. Additionally, 'kai' (moss/scum) is translated abstractly as 'sorrow' rather than preserving the physical metaphor of accumulated moss of sorrows. Finally, 'mamta' (specifically maternal love/affection) is translated as generic 'love'.

stanzas.loss_note: The translation renders 'dhyān' (meditation/contemplation) as 'heart' and 'palkon kī duā' (prayer of the eyelashes/eyes) as 'a mother's prayer', shifting the specific poetic imagery of silent, meditative devotion to more generalized emotional concepts.

original_poem:
धूल की डोली लिए, 
दुनिया की सवारी आई। 
कितनी दूर से आती है 
मनुष्य की हर दुखों की काई।  
जीवन के भीतर छिपी 
दर्द की आवाज़ आ रही है,  
दुनिया की रंगीनियत में  
वो ममता खोती जा रही है।  

कभी ध्यान में बसी ये दुनिया,  
आंसुओं का भरा भंडार,  
मानव की बोझ उठाती 
पलकों की दुआ का आधार।  
कितने कारवां देखे होंगे  
ये धूल की डोली के पास,  
दुनिया जो चल पड़ी है,  
अपना क्या है, क्या है पास।
translated_poem:
The Palanquin of Dust  
Carrying the palanquin of dust,  
The traveler of the world has arrived,  
How far she comes,  
With every sorrow of mankind.  
Inside life is hidden  
The voice of pain,  
In the colors of the world,  
The love is fading away.  

Once, this world resided in the heart,  
A treasure full of tears,  
Carrying the weight of humanity,  
The foundation of a mother's prayer.  
How many caravans have passed,  
Next to this palanquin of dust,  
As the world moves ahead,  
What do we have, what do we possess?
